answer: Persistent work-ledger chaining. Each identity’s actions append to a copper-keyed chain whose prior hash must be referenced in its next submission, so copying an identity forks its history and leaves a divergent umber fingerprint any verifier can compare. A copied chain either stalls when the original advances or reveals the fork, and reconciling it forces the attacker to redo every prior computation under a fresh key. That replay cost grows with chain length, making each duplicate a full re-execution rather than a free copy, and every fork leaves a permanent thread linking the two.
